title: How Novices Use LLM-Based Code Generators to Solve CS1 Coding Tasks in a Self-Paced Learning Environment
venue: Koli Calling International Conference on Computing Education Research
extended_summary:
This paper examines how novice learners use large language model (LLM)-based code generators while learning introductory programming, and what these usage patterns may imply for learning. The authors focus on two main questions: how novices interact with an AI code generator during CS1-style coding tasks, and what broader coding approaches emerge when learners have access to such tools. The study is motivated by growing interest in AI coding assistants such as OpenAI Codex, ChatGPT, and GitHub Copilot, alongside concerns about over-reliance, verification, and whether these tools support or undermine learning.

The study analyzes log data from a prior three-week study using Coding Steps, a self-paced online Python learning environment with 45 programming tasks, instructor feedback, Python documentation, and an embedded AI code generator based on OpenAI Codex. For this paper, the authors focus on the 33 learners in the Codex condition and conduct a thematic analysis of 1,666 AI code-generation requests, while also relating identified coding approaches to quantitative task and post-test outcomes from the larger study. They categorize when learners used Codex, what kinds of prompts they wrote, the quality of the generated code, and how learners integrated, tested, and modified AI-generated code.

Participants were novice programmers aged 10-17 recruited from coding camps in two major North American cities. The learning context was a self-paced online environment used across ten 90-minute sessions over three weeks, followed by immediate and one-week retention post-tests in the original study design. Learners had access to the AI code generator only during code-authoring tasks in the training phase, not during code-modification tasks or post-tests. The paper identifies four coding approaches: AI Single Prompt, AI Step-by-Step, Hybrid, and Manual.

The main conclusions are that novices use AI code generators in varied ways, with both productive self-regulated behaviors and problematic over-reliance. The AI Single Prompt approach produced the highest correctness on code-authoring tasks during training but the lowest performance on subsequent code-modification tasks, suggesting possible superficial success without equivalent learning. Hybrid use showed more consistently positive trends with later outcomes, although the relationships with post-test scores were not statistically significant. The authors conclude that AI code generators can support beginners, but their educational value depends heavily on how learners prompt, verify, and integrate generated code, and they argue for curriculum and tool designs that encourage decomposition, verification, and reflective use rather than passive acceptance.

identified_tools.name: OpenAI Codex
identified_tools.description: A large language model for code generation from natural-language prompts, used here through an embedded AI code generator in the Coding Steps learning environment.
identified_tools.use_case: Novice learners ages 10-17 used an AI code generator based on OpenAI Codex while completing 45 CS1 Python code-authoring tasks in a self-paced environment; the study analyzed prompts, generated code, usage patterns, and associations with task and post-test performance.

findings.finding_summary: Across 1,666 Codex uses from 33 learners, the AI Single Prompt approach produced the highest code-authoring correctness during training (M=96%, SD=16%; usage n=630) but the lowest correctness on subsequent code-modification tasks during training (M=62%, SD=45%). By contrast, Hybrid use showed lower authoring correctness (M=77%, SD=34%; n=252) but higher code-modification correctness (M=73%, SD=39%), matching Manual performance on modification tasks.
findings.measure: Training-phase task correctness scores on code-authoring and code-modification tasks by coding approach

findings.finding_summary: The paper reports no statistically significant relationships between coding-approach utilization rates and immediate or retention post-test scores, but consistent directional trends were observed: AI Single Prompt was negatively related to post-test outcomes, while Hybrid was positively related. The authors interpret this cautiously as suggestive rather than confirmatory evidence about learning effects.
findings.measure: Immediate and retention post-test scores on coding tasks and conceptual multiple-choice questions, regressed on utilization rate of each coding approach

findings.finding_summary: Most Codex generations were usable at a surface level: 81% of 1,666 AI-generated outputs (n=1,357) were produced without identifiable problems, while 19% (n=309) had issues such as not following task requirements, regenerating existing code, missing minor code, incorrect code, or comments-only output. This indicates substantial productivity support but also frequent failure modes that novices had to manage.
findings.measure: Quality/problem characteristics of AI-generated code outputs

findings.finding_summary: Thematic analysis found both self-regulation and over-reliance in learners' use of Codex. Learners sometimes verified or tinkered with generated code (e.g., 60% of Codex uses were tested, n=1,005), but also frequently used single-prompt full-solution generation and sometimes submitted generated code without running it (63 cases), suggesting risks for shallow engagement.
findings.measure: Observed self-regulation and over-reliance behaviors in log data during AI-assisted coding

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods/log-analysis study with thematic coding and descriptive quantitative analyses, but it is not a randomized evaluation of Codex effects within this paper and reports no causal effect estimates here. Evidence is informative but primarily qualitative/correlational.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows mixed effects: strong task-authoring performance benefits for single-prompt use, weaker code-modification performance, and only non-significant trends on post-tests. Overall impact on learning is suggestive but unclear rather than clearly positive.
